title: Jersey Economics: How Mumbai Indians Can Turn Identity into Merchandise Demand
dek: A shirt sells when fans see themselves in it. The players who stay longest are the faces of Mumbai Indians' identity, and the data shows who they are.
excerpt: Mumbai Indians have used many players, but a small core of long-serving names did a large share of the scoring. Those are the identities a jersey is built around.
author: CricField Editorial Desk

sections.heading: Identity Is Built on Continuity
body: Merchandise demand follows attachment, and attachment grows with time. A player who wears the shirt for many seasons becomes part of how fans describe the team.
{{ev:je-used}} players have batted or bowled for Mumbai Indians. Only {{ev:je-long}} of them played five or more seasons for the franchise.

sections.heading: The Faces of the Franchise
body: Those long-serving players scored {{ev:je-share}} of Mumbai Indians' runs. {{ev:je-name}} leads with {{ev:je-seasons}} seasons; the chart lists the longest-serving players.
These are the names most likely to carry the jersey's identity, and the ones a franchise loses most by letting go.

sections.heading: From Identity to Demand
body: Turning identity into merchandise demand is a retail question: range, pricing, channels and timing around retention news and big fixtures.

sections.heading: What the Warehouse Cannot See
body: The CricField warehouse is ball-by-ball cricket data. It contains no merchandise sales, pricing or retail-channel data, so it cannot measure the commercial side of this question directly.
Testing the link between player continuity and shirt sales would need sales by season and by printed name.

sections.heading: CricField Verdict: Keep the Faces
body: Mumbai Indians' identity has rested on a small group of long-serving players. Retention decisions should weigh the identity value of those players, not only their output.
Measuring that value properly needs retail data that this warehouse does not hold.
